projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harry Dombrowski was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the old history of World War II veteran Harry F. Dombrowski. Mr. Dombrowski served in the U.S. Army. He served in the European Theater, and his highest rank was PFC. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Dombrowski's home in Brooklyn, Ohio on February 26th, 2003. Harry was 80 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Okie, dokie. Well, what it was, I was with the 30th Infantry Division, Fourth--Company I, Fourth Platoon, Fourth Squad. I was a machine gunner. I had awards in expert machine gunning, M-1 rifle, and also with a .45 pistol. I went in the Battle of the Bulge, December 16th. My commander was Colonel General Hodge. He was the commander of the 30th Division, and I had a Lieutenant Colonel Herland commander was the First Battalion of 119th. We woke up that morning--didn't wake up, we never slept with that snow and whatnot. But we got there, and we heard this terrific noise coming, and we looked, there comes a panzer. We were really shocked. They got upon us pretty doggone fast. As we were taken prisoners, I took my rifle, I mean, my .45 and dismantled and threw it all around so that they could not use it. I got rid of my pistol, all my ammunition belt and threw them out. I turned around and lo and behold I looked in the woods behind me, and all I could see was tracer shells coming from the panzer division tanks. And I've seen many of our boys being wounded with these tracers. That must have been something fierce because I know tracers, they are hot. Well, they took us and marched us down the street down there to a house and told us to go down in the basement. Well, all of us went down in the basement and couldn't find room, but we got there. We stayed there, I don't know how long, but they took my wrist watch away from me, and took everything away from me. And what happened is I had pictures of the Messerschmitt airplane. I had it in my helmet. Dumb me, didn't think about it, but they seen it, and they beat the hell out of me because I had that, and they asked me where I got it. And I said, I found it back there. They said, where? I said, next to town someplace, I couldn't tell you the village. Well, they beat the hell out of me. Okay. Then I come back, and we stay there, and stayed there awhile. All of a sudden they go to interview everybody. They took 20 of us. We went to this Vonstead, he was interrogating us. He asked you your name, where you lived, what city you lived, what were you doing there? Alls I did was remember my instructions, Harry--PFC Harry Dombrowski, 355-14-669. He kept asking my, this and that, and I said: Harry Dombrowski, 355-14-669. Well, he got tired of it, and I got one in the back of the head, and I really went down there. And I explained to them, boom, again I got it. He took me back. You stay back there again, and lo and behold it wasn't, I don't know, I didn't know hours from minutes, minutes from days or what. But anyhow, here comes one German, herauskommen, herauskommen, that meant come out of the cellar. And I said, oh, geez. He says, herauskommen. We got out of the cellar all right. And he hollered herauskommen again and threw a hand grenade in there. There was, I know there was, somewhere I felt it, and I come out. They stayed there. I know they are still there. Well, they moved us down, and that night they stood us up, and they took so many men out of there, and we had to go out in the field to take care of their dead. We did that. We took dog tags, put them on the, American dog tags on the Germans, and we took uniforms, they said put them on the dead for census. Well, then we also hauled ammunition. My very bad thing about that was, I did not like doing what I was doing because I was doing stuff that they were killing our boys with. And again, three of us really got knocked out of us. We went on the ground, we got a good kick in the rear end, and kick in the stomach, and they know, it was a panzer division, and them guys don't play around. I mean, they are strictly government. Young guys, too. What I would like to know, I often think today, when I walk down the street, or I'm at a meeting someplace, and I hear German people talking. My Dad was German and my Mother was German. But I often wonder, where were they in World War II? Am I talking to you now and at that time you were shooting at me? Well, I don't know, but I still rebel it. Anyhow, do you have--know how many people were wounded, American wounded over there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, you can go ahead and mention that.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Five thousand Americans; fifty-five thousand British; six thousand Germans. Six hundred thousand Germans were there. We had two hundred thousand casualties; eighty-one thousand Americans; ninety-one thousand nine hundred killed in action. Twenty-three thousand were prisoners. British, fourteen thousand six hundred casualties were killed or wounded. Germans, one hundred thousand killed or wounded. And crazy enough, I don't know if you've been out to Western Reserve Cemetery yet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, I haven't been there, no.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: We dedicated a beautiful monument to the Battle of the Bulge that's got all the listings of all the dead and whatnot, what it cost. Like I say, Lieutenant Colonel, he was commander of First Battalion, the 19th Infantry. The worst part about that is I hear--I knew we were being replenished with more boys, more men. They tell me they had to replenish the 30th four times. Not only four times, I knew no one. You never got to know anybody because they were going there, going there, going there. One minute you'd be talking to them, the next minute they are laying there. And it's sad to say that you were in a company, it was a good one, the 30th Division, but yet you didn't know anybody, and I regret that today. I think when I came home, after Battle of the Bulge and everything was over with, I think I did come over to the 30th. I don't know. We were there, they are not--the 82nd Airborne, we were there December 16th, and I was held prisoner, I think it was for eight days. Again, I'm not sure as the time end date, but I'm sure it was after Christmas, and I was happy to get out. Well, when we got back --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How did you get freed?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: The 82nd Airborne came in and they really got in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you were being detained near the front line there then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. We were sent back to the line there, and I don't know who it was, but the ones that were left, that came back as prisoners were--had to stand there, and stand at attention, and this guy got up there, a colonel or a general or whatever he was, and called us a bunch of yellow--I know we're the best--and I hope he is looking upstairs now because he couldn't go to heaven. He was full of hell.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he lined up the former POWs and lectured them for being captured?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And what the hell could we do? They out ran us. We seen that. They came from all over. You know, I bet you he'd never seen, like the SF panzer, what they did to our guys was something fierce. They shot them, I know they shot them. We took, like I was saying, they took us out at night to handle their dirty work. Well, knock on wood I was one of the fortunate ones. They took us out, and this one kid took us someplace else. We had to do, move bodies over, and the rest of the guys went somewhere else, and alls I could hear was that machine gunner of theirs going. And the only ones that came back was the ones that took care of the dead. The rest were, most of them were all killed, by German panzers. All in all we seen the bodies of dead Americans run over by tanks. And you talk about a bloody sight. Did you ever see a human being flat as a pancake? I've seen several of them. I just, my heart went out to them, and still today it lays in my guts what they done to us. I know when we captured them, them guys, they come over here and lived like King of Pharuke in Carson City. I know that very well. But today it lies in my guts what they did to us, and I don't want to go through it again. Our food, while we were prisoners, we had one potato and one cigarette per ten men, and that was it. We were lucky to get that. If you had to go to the bathroom while you were a prisoner, you had to go when ten other guys had to go. You take your helmet outside, or go someplace out in the field, and that cold weather, huh-uh, no, it was fierce. I feel sorry for the boys. And how else can I say it except that was the Battle of the Bulge which I will live through and through and through and never forget it. And again, I felt bad because I don't know what happened to the 30th Infantry, whether they--I hate--I see letters and everything but morally I don't know. I wanted to go to the reunion but I didn't get there as of yet due to health reasons.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So do you still think you feel some resentment toward Germans?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, I really do. I mean, I wonder how many of them guys that we talked to, where they were because you could spot them like-- [Interview interrupted by telephone call].

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you want to continue or should we--I can--we can start earlier if you'd like.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: 1941 I lived in Palmer Heights, 6659 Pearl Road.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: I was 20, went in the service when I was 21.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you drafted then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: You know, I was working at the Palmer Theater as a--well, I was head usher there, and that afternoon we had our movie going on, and all of a sudden my boss come out and he says, hey. I said, what? He said, the Japanese just bombed Pearl Harbor, and the whole damn show went in a frizzy. That was hard to stomach. I couldn't picture people coming from way over there to way over here and bombing us and tearing the hay out of it. And it was just unforgettable, unforgettable.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did it come as a total surprise to you then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah, very much. I didn't think they could do it. Well, we never had thoughts of them coming over here and bombing our--getting rid of us. A great place like they had, but we didn't know very much about Japan. I know we were selling steel to them and we were getting that back in a different way, but then they started drafting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: And everybody had to go, so everybody had to go then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: In '42. I went to Camp Perry, I was up there. It took us, I don't know how long by train to get up to that joint. I mean, it's not that far, but it took us a long time. They talk about, they got four to eight male car in France. Hey, I think we had the same thing over here, whether or not we were right for it. There I stayed three days, and then they put our boarders on another train, and we headed south to Fort Bragg, North Carolina. That's where I got my training, basic training.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any memorable stories from your basic training?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No, not too much. It was colder than hell down there, I mean, we are used to that, but so what? Not like what it was like in the Battle of the Bulge. I never had weather like that, rain, snow. People talk about it, they are fighting about this right now. Them guys--them last guys had it rough over there, darn rough. Not like the guys today, and we did not have the technology like the Army's got today. The infantryman is just about gone here. It's all technology. And our planes are all technology. Our bombs were and whatnot. But I don't like to see anything coming right now because it's not going to be good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was it like when you reported to basic training and you were thrown into a situation with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: It was--we got to know one another over there in basic, and we cooperated with everybody. It was rough, but not as rough as the Marine Corp. I mean, we were walking and hiking and what the hellnot, but that's all I was--I kind of enjoyed it. We did not get to go to town because we were frozen there. We never did have a furlough. And after we left there we went to Camp Patrick Henry, Virginia, and there it was cold and muddy. It was a brand new camp. We slept in mud. We ate in mud and everything else was pure mud because it was brand new. And December 25th, they played "I'll Dream of a White Christmas", and I was walking up the gangplank to go someplace. Dressed in heavy clothes and whatnot. I thought we were going to Europe. We did not go to Europe; we went to Panama. Everybody was making a bet with us to where we were going, nobody knew, but as we got on the ship and we were going, it was getting warmer and warmer. This is not going to Europe, I said, I don't know where the hell we are going now. I spent two years, almost--about a year and a half, not quite a year down in Panama.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were you doing in Panama?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: We were jungle--we went down there for jungle training, and that's all--I got a different kind of a training than what we are used to. Hotter than hell. The rain. The humidity was sky high. You had to live with snakes, and who the hellnot, wild boars. They thought about it. And one day when we took a 25 mile field marches, and we walked all through the jungle, and that one place they told us to load our guns with live ammunition because they were full of wild boars and they do attack. And I said, Jesus Christ, what the hell else. But we had one colonel, Lieutenant Thompson, he was a chubby guy, don't get me wrong. He's a chubby guy, but he couldn't keep up with us. If you fell behind, he'd hit you in the rear end with a damn sword. But he finally pooped out on us, and we left him way behind. He got diarrhea. I don't know what happened to him, but he didn't come back into camp with us. Then the other thing is, we were guarding the canal, and every so often you had to go, go to two hours on, four off. At night it was a corker because you couldn't look over the canal and watch everything going on. They said ships, strange ships may come in and try to bomb them. Well, that night we were on, and all of a sudden this darn second Lieutenant Nord, he come in, he snuck around real quiet like to see if we were sleeping. Well, he did that three times. The fourth time he got it. We took cans and put them on the trees and on the ground, and they were traps. He didn't know about them, but he comes out--you know what happened to him. Then we sent the--the other thing is we were guarding the canal by going through the canal on boats, which was good because that was good duty. Geez, man, I'd go all the time for a load of that. And then they told us we were--that was the 14th Infantry. Well, then they told us again, we are going to go back to the United States. We're going in the 71st Division. They didn't tell us where, but we are going back. So away we went. Well, we got to Camp Carson, Colorado and there they told us we were the 71st Division. We are going to be training down there. But down there during--during the day was nice, but at night it was cold. It was right by--I forgot the name of that air base down there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Lowery?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Something like that. But they used to take us out at night on desert training, and these places come over here at night and scare the living hell out of us. And this one liberter, he came over that night, but I don't know what he was doing, but he missed us by ten miles. He hit the damn mountain. He blew up. I said, you jerk.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, he hit the mountain?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, that plane just went--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow, that's a B-24?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. I don't know how he--why he missed it. He had the coordinations wrong. It wasn't right. Well, then from there we went to Camp Hale up in the mountains, sky trips up there. We helped them out. We studied under them. We traveled up there. I don't know how many times in that deep snow, we slept in snow, ate in snow and everything else. Well, they told us we were going to California, Monterey, California. What else are they going to do now? We got there, I think it was the 10th Mountaineers. We learned to live with mules. The mules were treated better than us. They had six hours with that pack on, and if you kept them more than six hours on a pack, you were court martialed. No, they were pride and joy, and up the mountain, down the mountain, around the mountain. Them guys could make it. Well, word came through they were going to have volunteers for ETO. Well, let's get out of this joint and do something. So I volunteered for ETO. I got it. They gave me a 30 day leave, and I came home for 30 days. I didn't tell my mother and dad where I was going. I went back and I got there, I was there only three days, and they shipped me to Baltimore. From Baltimore I went across the ETO.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So about when did you make that crossing?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: That crossing was--I got into France June 17th, and there it started all over, all the way up from Saint Lowe probably to Bastone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you cross right and landed at France, you didn't land in the UK or Great Britain?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No--oh, beg your pardon, I did go to Britain, Birmingham.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Birmingham? So how long were you in Britain?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: I was there two weeks, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Two weeks?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Then we boarded the boats to go over. And dumb me, you know, the landing board, we went out and there was a channel, and I looked over, and I said, I'm on the wrong damn boat, I know that. So I told him, and he says, yeah, you are. He said, we have to get you over to the other boat, so they got me over to the other boat and we got to Normandy all right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you with the 30th Division then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah. That's when I joined up with them. We joined up with them, and we went up to Saint Lowe, fall through the hedges. We got to Saint Lowe, that was a tough battle up there because you couldn't pick nothing, and we were there. At night we had a place there, a house, and there were stairs going up, and we had a little window, we could see the Germans on across the courtyard there. I said, well, geez. They did tell us do not smoke or ____ because they could spot a light. Well, they called upon me to go get some sea rations. We went out at night and brought, I don't know how many cases of sea rations back to us so we could eat. Well, we got back there--well, I was suppose to be back to the help poster. I couldn't see anything. I said, what happened to him? He said, nothing; he's dead. He lit a cigarette, but he got it right in the head. I said, oh Christ. Then I said, I'm going down. We went down again. About 3:00 o'clock and all tired is herauskommen, herauskommen, herauskommen, means come on out. Those Germans were begging us to come out of that house. They wanted to take us prisoner. Well, we told them, go to hell, and then I opened the door and let them have it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, he was actually standing outside trying to get you to surrender to them?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. That's the end of him. But then I went on, we got through at Saint Lowe, and July 31st, another one of my members, my sisters. I don't know if you know what a machine gun weighs or not, if you've ever carried one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've never carried one.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Well, they told us we were going to make an attack with this machine gun. It weighs over 90 something pounds, and you've got four crew. One carries the machine gun, the other carries the extra barrel, and the other ones carry the ammunition. I said, I've never heard of this damn thing. So we had to load the gun up, put it on lock, and I was the one that carried the damn thing. We got to hedges, to hedge road, we run like hell up there. I was beat, that thing was heavy. I got up there, and my fingers slipped and knocks it off the lock and I had one fire, but my captain told me, don't ever do that again. I said, I didn't mean it. He said, I don't give a shit. I said, well, I said I'm sorry. And just then, there it is, the first wound I got. That was, now I know what a bullet feels like when it goes into a body. It's hot. Well, I told them, I says--he says, go back, get out of here. We'll take it. You can't help. When I got back I went to England. They patched my arm up, and I came back, landed in France again, and they're short drivers, so they looked at me, well, do you drive a truck, too? I said, yeah. So we go--so we had to carry ammunition. They had a car, a two by four--not a two by four, they call them--I forgot what they call them right now. Well, I drove that thing from France all the way to Belgium to rejoin my group, the 30th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how long were you recuperating from that wound then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: It was about a month and a half, maybe a month and a half, and then I joined my group and I stayed with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that your first day of combat when you were wounded or near it?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No, that was my--I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah. I was never taught to kill anybody. I was never taught, and I don't like guns today. I do not want a gun around here, and I wouldn't have them. But I used a machine gun, and I know that it spits fire out, and I had to learn to use it very, very good, and I got expert marksman with that. But again I wouldn't want it, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What is it like that first day when you were under fire?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Well, to see somebody walking ahead of you, or running, or dodging you, and to pull that trigger and then see them how they [groans] And down they go. That took a lot away from me, but it's either you or him. It didn't make no difference. You or him had to do it, and I said, well, it's not going to be me. So that was that, and I learned to control my composure or what, to live, know I had to do what I had--what I just did. Again, I don't want to do it no more.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that your job most of the time, part of the machine gun crew?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah. The last time, yeah, after I had got captured in Belgium, Battle of the Bulge, they took us back and we were down in a hospital two days, and the V-2 bombs were coming in, but it hit close by, the V-2 bombs, but didn't bother us. But then they sent us back to our outfit again. All together, new men again. Nobody knew nothing. Nobody knew anybody. I don't know how these commanders got away with it. I don't know, but they did. Then we were going, and I was leading up, and I told my boys, I had the machine gun again. I was carrying it up the hill, and my crew was behind me. I turned around, and I hollered, I says, I told you once, I'll tell you again, if you don't listen to me this time, don't blame me what you get. And just as I said that, a mortar shell comes in and, yeah, you know what happened? I got it in the leg. The rest of the guys got it, and they're still there. They're probably home now, but rest their souls.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other memories of the Camp David Normandy?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No. Yeah. This was my second wound. I had one more to go. Then we were coming up to Callone, and Callone Contadro on the Rhine. Beautiful. We watched this priest go by every night. _______+ he's a priest, he's a man of the card. Well, we watched him when he walked by. He went in the cathedral, and we go fine. But when he was up at the steeple, we got a volley of--a barrage of artillerian ________+. They knew right where we were. Here he was a German, dressed as a priest. And we got to watching him, and a member of the debtor squad pictured him and found him where he was, which window he was at, and he got him. So that ended that. No, not of good worries, a lot of good memories, but they're--I can't say good memories but memories that you live with. Oh, the other one was at Saint--but I'll go back to Saint Lowe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Every night they had a German plane come over, every night at 11:00 o'clock. We called him Bedtime Charlie, and he would fly over us and fly over us and fly, and he would drop the flares and look to see what he's got down there. And we were all instructed, don't even look up when you see him. Forget it, don't even hear him. Well, everybody finally did it. He never did get anybody. That's a good memory, and that's how it lives with me when I came home. And when I came home I was, what do they call it, battle fatigue. We were relatives. I would list those, and every night a plane would fly over here. I'd dive under the bed and beat the hell out of somebody who was there. I had a hell of a time. And they sent me downtown, and I was under the VA care for quite awhile. They examined me and put me in, they give me the truth serum. And I was there, I don't know how many weeks with that truth serum. You know, I sodium pent up my arm, and we love it there. You can talk. You don't know you're talking, but you do talk. And I have one boy with me right now, he lives with me. He's a 14 year old kid. He's a German soldier. I had an annihilation with a piano wire. I put it around his neck and that was it. He was walking by me, and he spotted me, and I was faster than him. I guess he was quite entrained. He pulled a gun, and I took the piano wire and put it around his neck. Well, like I say, he's still with me. He's still with me. He follows me all over. He don't bother me, so I don't bother him. Now, that's about all I got.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did that happen in Germany then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you caught up with your unit in Belgium. When was that in relation to the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: I would say that was the end of November.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any memories of anything before the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No, except that we were fighting, still fighting, city to city, Leiage, and all them, building to building. A lot of things happened there. Artillery for both ends. We had the war and artilleries. Our artillery men, they had it worked out where they'd keep firing, and after each shell they'd raise their _____. So when they did fire a shell would land over here and jumped on over the fence. That was a good set up right there. The food was--again people hollering about this weather. Hey, this weather is mild compared to that. I mean, we were knee high in snow, and we slept in this damn stuff. We ate in it. We did not take no baths. We didn't have--and I know a lot of fellas who got frostbite on their legs. When they'd pull their socks off, their skin came right with it. In fact, one of our commanders of our--the Battle of the Bulge right now, it's his legs that were frozen. When they took his shoes off, everything else came along with it. And we had socks on. I couldn't tell you how long we had the same pair of socks on, but they were a long time. Same shoes, same pants, same shorts. We were--same gotsies, but we lived with them, we only fought with them, and a lot of men died with them. Not very many of our guys are, of the whole Battle of the Bulge are still with us. There is no doubt, you know, the old soldiers are kind of dwindling. In fact, I just buried three of them. I was telling my wife, I said, well, I've got a big string. That string is getting shorter and shorter. This is true. I'm 80, and we just buried my good friend. He was 82. He was a P-51, a pilot in Germany, and I never knew he was a pilot until we buried him. He never did--we never did talk about, you know, the war and stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you captured, to recap--was it the first or second day of the Bulge you were captured?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, it was the second day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Second day?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. We got out there--I never want to see--I look at another damn tank the way I seen that tank coming up on the hill there, and there it was. It was as big as a mountain. Holy, Jesus. Oy, oy, oy. And he was firing his machine gun like crazy, that turd was just busy. Between him, the machine gun and his torque gun, he just played hell with our men. And I, like I said before, I turned around, I looked at our men running up the hill, and how many of those men got tracer shells in their back. Oh, Jesus. And, of course, I couldn't stop to think about it. I thought, why couldn't we help them? But we know we couldn't, no, huh-uh, no. So when we were captured we had to do their dirty work. We had to move their dead. Move it, change their uniforms, put our dog tags on them, on the ones that were laying in the field there that we didn't get to. They changed that and whatnot and so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many guys were captured with you?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: There were 275 of us captured, and I think I would have taken 275. Everybody's ____ would come back. I couldn't tell you how many came back because--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Whereabouts was that again, that you were captured?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: That was in the Battle of the Bulge near Malmody.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was near Malmody.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No. My own crew, my machine gun crew that I was telling you about, I did not know their first name. I couldn't tell you their first name because I never heard of them. Everybody was--I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before, early on did you have any close buddies?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Oh, I had some, Tom. Don't ask me their last name because I couldn't tell you. George. We got along very, very good, and we knew what was going on. To tell where they are at today is, I hope they are still living. I know--I'm trying to get, we're going to write to somebody from the Battle of the Bulge Magazine and find out where my division, where it is. Old Hickory, that was the 30th. That was the one with the blue and the red and the three crosses in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you came back after you were wounded, you were still with the 30th, though, right?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, you're saying that during that time that you were wounded a lot of guys left the outfit one way or another?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you don't know what happened with that?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No, huh-uh, huh-uh, no. Never knew them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when you came back there were a lot of new faces?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any memories of mail call, getting packages from home, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: The only place we got mail is in England. From France on up we didn't get no mail whatsoever, never, huh-uh, no way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Red Cross packages. Anything?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Nothing, nothing. And that's the honest to goodness truth. I did not even receive one postcard from nobody.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you try to write back home?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: I wrote one letter to my Mother and Dad and told them I was all right, not to worry, and that's the only one I wrote. I didn't have pencil or paper. As strange as it seems, I never knew that a death letter was white with a black border. That is--well, I found some letters in a German house with black borders. [Interview interrupted by dog barking.]

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: We were talking about your writing letters?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah. I, like I say, I did not know about black and white. So in this house I found this, and I found a pencil. So I wrote a letter to my Dad and Mom and told them, I'm all right, and sent it on. Well, they told me, I said, what the hell are you doing? The guy next door to me he says, do you know what you sent? I says, yeah, a letter to my Dad. He said, what kind of paper? I said, black and white. He said, you shouldn't have sent black and white because that means dead.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when they got that envelope they thought uh-oh.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah. She won't bite you. She's just nosy as hell. Maybe I should take their bag and take their picture. Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any kind of entertainment over there? Did you see any shows or anything?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: I've never seen a USO show. How they got--I think those were the ones in the back echelon that seen those, not the front--we didn't have time to go showboating. We were at--I think it was Leiage. They did pull us off the front line and take us back to Leiage. There was a coal mine there. It was huge with all kinds of showers. That's the first time we took a shower and changed, got a new change of clothing. And those showers are--oh, hell, they're not compared to this city here. You had to pull this chain down and the water came down. Bathroom facilities, that's the first time we had bathroom facilities. Otherwise the rest was all outside in the woods. The ground was well fertilized over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So anything else that you remember? Let's see, you were back with the outfit after you got liberated from being a prisoner, after about what, eight days you say? So that would have been, what would you say about the--

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: It was after Christmas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the Battle of the Bulge went on for another month?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, in January. It last till January.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other memories when you got back with your outfit?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No, no memories.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Then you continued on, I assume, with the 30th?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, but all new people, all new faces, all new everything, and when we got--where was it. We left for home after everything was over with, out of France, the border of Bolter. That's another thing, all those guys here got a big rip roaring stand off a base in New York City. I don't know if they were in a war or not because we didn't see none of this stuff. We never had a chance to see none of this stuff. And we got to New York, off the boat, into a train, into a train to Indian Town Gap, and our discharge papers. They ask you if I want to sign up again? I said, you're nuts. They were going to give us three hundred dollars for a reenlistment right then and there. Not me, I'm going home. And they came and paid me and I got my discharge. I got the first bus to Indian Town Gap where the trains were, the depot there. Got on a train, come home. I woke my Dad and Mom up at 3:00 o'clock in the morning. I'm home here down by the Erie Station down there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Well, I was--we had tears and whatnot. My Dad was not very emotional about nothing. He's seen it, and I knew in his eyes that he was glad to see me home. Because out of eight kids, I was the only one that had to go and serve in the service. And I don't regret serving, I'm very, very proud of being in the uniform, and I don't know if I went on a two day road and then had to do it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you come home then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: That was November 25th, '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you a part of the occupation forces in Germany?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No, no. I got into a boat--I mean, into a train, on a train to Moharve, boarded a boat there and came across.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was then shortly after VE day then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yep. END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you do anything to celebrate VE day?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No, no. No, I just took it like an ordinary day, and that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were, when you were still in Europe the rumors were that you might be headed for --

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In the Pacific? What was the reaction there?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: I didn't lie, I was very, very teed off about that. I did my duty over here, I paid for it. I'm going to join that outfit now? I ain't going to Japan, no way, huh-uh, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So where were you when they dropped the first Teutonic bomb?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: I think I was, I'm trying to think now. To tell you the truth, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Somewhere in Europe?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Somewhere, someplace, somehow.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any reaction when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Well, I said, why in the hell didn't they do it a long time ago? It's just the same as I feel about Iraq right now. We should have stayed there and finished that damn battle instead of doing what we did. Of course, who am I to say that, I don't want to be accused of saying, but that's my reaction, I mean, and just what my thoughts are. We should have stayed at that--now we are going to have to do it again, and more of our fellas are going to be--that's the sad part about it. Again, I didn't mean anything about it but that's my own thoughts.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were still there probably on VJ-day, obviously?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, because wasn't it--Roosevelt died in April.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Do you remember that, that was like April 12th of '45?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Somewhere in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were--the war was still going on?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing --

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: We heard about it, yeah. Yeah. I'm trying to think, well, where the hell was I then? We were in Germany, I mean, it's somewhere over there, more or less Belgium or--yeah Belgium.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You might have been in Germany at that point?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, somewhere.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were across the Rhine at that point?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction when you heard about FDR passing?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: We took it very bad. I know I did. To me he was a fine gentleman. Of course, I'm not no politician, but I enjoyed him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did the guys think about Truman?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: They didn't think too much about him. In other words, again, we said, well, let's see what the hell he can do. And there was not very much political talk about it. But we did feel bad about Roosevelt. We didn't feel bad about his wife, but we felt bad about him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the guys weren't really sure if Truman was up for the job?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: They were not sure, but then they found out. So that's about all that I know, Tom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience over there, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah. I still can see my squad, the machine gun squad going down. Like I told them, do not group up, and no sooner than I said that, I turned and walked away and "shoo" and that's all there was to it. And the "shoo" was that mortar that came in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that was three guys that got it?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah. The one guy was carrying the actual barrel, he was up there with me. And I can remember, as soon as I said that I turned around and walked up. And the other one was, oh, I have, you know, that was up in Belgium, too. That's when I got my leg.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was your third one?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me about that then?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: I got it, and I went up near, I know, and the damn gun came down someplace. But anyhow, I felt that. I turned and I seen my boys, what was left of them, but there was nothing I could do. But I crawled up to a tank up there, one of our tanks, I crawled underneath it. This lieutenant was standing who lived there. He said, hey you, get your butt upstairs, you're going to operate this tank. I said, I can't go no damn place. He said, why? He said, you disobey? I said, yes, I am. I am wounded. Can you see this leg? You can't fire that gun? I said, no. I said, where the hell is a medical station at anyhow? He said, how the hell do I know? I'm a tank commander. Well, he says, I think if you'll go down the road down there, you'll run into them. Well, I started down there. I put a belt around my blooden so it wouldn't bleed. I walked, hobbled down there, and I found me a medic, and he told me to lay down there. He got a stretcher and another guy come up and they carried me to the first aid station. But that was a good thing, I mean, I didn't mind it. You know what they gave me? A good shot of vodka. Man, that knocked me right out. And the next thing I was, I was on a train going towards France again. So that was then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when about was that?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Oh, that was the year at the end of the war right now, Tom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were out of commission for the rest of the war at that point or did you go back to your unit?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Well, I did go back to my unit. I did go back to my unit again. And again in the room, and I'm still going--like I say, write to my, this Battle of the Bulge and find out where we are. Because maybe I would like to go down to a reunion some time and see them. I know this coming Sunday I'm going to a Purple Heart Conference in Columbus with George Doyle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. George --

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, he's good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Also, let's see, the first time you were wounded that was in France, and that was a bullet wound?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yes, at Saint Lowe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Second time was the mortar hit?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that was about when? Was that before you were captured or after?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: That was before, before, yeah, before. Before I was captured.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how long were you recuperating from that wound?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: That was--they heal one pretty fast over there. They did not baby you, I mean, you're in the hospital, and not like here, boom. And then the third one was after that, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was in the spring of '45?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you took three Purple Hearts?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yep. And then that's about all I know right now, Tom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other decorations or anything you want to mention? Did you get a Bronze Star?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, it sounds like you should have gotten a Bronze Star.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It sounds like you should have gotten a Bronze Star.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Actually you got--you probably got a combat--no, were you infantry?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Yeah, I got a combat--yeah, oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I may be mistaken, but I think you're due a Bronze Star if you have the Combat Infantry Badge. Maybe they changed that.

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: Well, I probably--I've got them upstairs somewhere. I went to, one of my good friends he just passed away, just buried him last week. He had 13 caps, in the DAV, VFW, Battle of the Bulge. What the hell else? I looked at them, but I didn't pay no attention to them. Finally, I finally talked to somebody about it, he says, yeah, he belonged to this, he belonged to that, he belonged to that, but he never attended them. He belonged to a Purple Heart, we had Purple Hearts here, and George Doyle's in my right, he's my commander. And Fred belonged to the Purple Heart, and he lives here in Warren, Ohio, but he never went. Now, he had double of everything. And he had all his badges on in the casket with him, all kinds of badges, whatever, I don't know. One guy says, what's that for? I go, he probably went someplace. Yeah, he had the Bronze Star, too. So I gots mine upstairs someplace. Every now and then I go up there and look. No, that Battle of the Bulge was your greatest battle of all. That even beat, that even beat Pearl Harbor. That beat World War I. That was the biggest battle that ever was done. But the way those Germans were going to do it, they were on their way to Hamsburg where the gas was. That's what they were heading for because they were running out of gas, and a lot of their tanks that they came up with were already out of gas. And boy, if we wouldn't have stopped them then, you know, I don't know where we would be today.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there a point where you thought maybe you might lose the Battle of the Bulge? Did it look pretty bleak?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: To some respects, yeah, but then again we had a good, a bunch of good, we had a good troop, we had a good Army. And they knew what they were doing, from the paratroopers to the guards, they came in there on the Battle of the Bulge. Them guys had it rough, the fighter pilots. Well, Tom, there's nothing else.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Harry Dombrowski
sp.p: I think it did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.
